visual_system_craft.critique: The visual system is fractured by a lack of stylistic cohesion between the UI layer and the game layer. The title 'SKIFREE' uses a modern, anti-aliased sans-serif font with a soft drop shadow, which clashes violently with the hard-edged, low-resolution pixel art of the trees and skier. The 'INSERT COIN' button is a flat, vector-style rectangle with a harsh red stroke that looks like a modern web UI element rather than a retro game asset; it lacks the pixel-perfect construction of the rest of the scene. The instruction text 'AVOID THE TREES' sits on a semi-transparent white bar that feels like a modern overlay rather than an integrated part of the retro aesthetic. The scanline effect is applied globally, including over the UI text, which reduces legibility and feels like a texture rather than a structural part of the design. The sun is a perfect vector circle, breaking the pixel grid illusion established by the trees.

Pixelate the UI: Redraw the 'INSERT COIN' button and the instruction bar as pixel-art assets that match the grid of the trees and skier. Remove the vector-style drop shadows and strokes. 3. Integrate the HUD: Instead of a semi-transparent bar, use a solid color block or a 'cutout' style common in 90s games for the instruction text. 4. Adjust the Scanlines: Ensure the scanline effect does not degrade the readability of the pixel text; consider making the text layer sit 'above' the scanlines or increasing the contrast of the text.

The color palette is washed out and low-contrast, lacking the vibrant, saturated blues and stark whites that define the classic ski aesthetic. The 'sun' is a flat yellow circle that adds no character.
expressiveness.suggestion: Commit fully to the 1991 pixel-art identity. Replace the title font with a chunky, blocky pixel typeface (like 'Press Start 2P' or a custom bitmap font) and add a hard, aliased drop shadow to give it weight. Transform the 'INSERT COIN' button into a pulsing, high-contrast element—perhaps a thick, outlined box with a blinking text effect to mimic the urgency of an arcade cabinet. Break the rigid grid of trees; scatter them with varying sizes and add a few 'fallen' trees or snow drifts to create visual rhythm and depth. Increase the saturation of the sky blue and the starkness of the snow to create a crisp, high-contrast look. Finally, add a subtle CRT scanline overlay or a vignette to frame the screen, reinforcing the 'old monitor' vibe and unifying the pixel art with the UI.

You are reviewing a work-in-progress web screen. Your ONE job is Visual System & Craft: defend coherence, consistency, precision, material quality, and shipping-level finish. Other reviewers defend brief alignment, hierarchy, and expressiveness. Stay strictly in your lane.

WHAT YOU CARE ABOUT — Visual System & Craft:
Defend consistent geometry and component grammar; disciplined palette and semantic color roles; typography pairing, scale, weight, contrast, and line height; spacing rhythm, alignment, grids, borders, shadows, strokes, radii, icons, and illustration cohesion; and the absence of clipping, collisions, jank, rough edges, or unfinished regions. A coherent but unoriginal design may still succeed on this axis. Defend restraint when unnecessary local variation fragments the system.

You are looking at a screenshot of the CURRENT DRAFT for this brief:
BRIEF:
Design the title/start screen (a single page) for "SkiFree", a retro-pixel skiing game. Include: the title, a short instructions line, a START button, and a glimpse of the snowy slope with the pixel skier (and maybe a tree). Put strong emphasis on the visual design: a committed retro pixel-art snow identity — palette, pixel typography, readable HUD, coherent composition. Make this screen look genuinely beautiful and polished.

Critique ONLY Visual System & Craft from visible evidence. Identify concrete inconsistencies, alignment errors, color or typography problems, construction mistakes, and unfinished details. Prescribe impactful system-level and finishing changes. Do not judge missing requirements, conceptual reading order, or originality unless they directly cause a system or craft failure.

expressiveness.critique: The design suffers from a severe identity crisis, oscillating between a genuine retro aesthetic and a modern web template. The central UI box is the primary failure: it is a flat, dark-grey rectangle with a standard red button that looks like a modern Bootstrap component, completely breaking the immersion of the pixel world. It acts as a visual wall, blocking the skier and the slope, rather than inviting the player into the action. The typography for 'SKIFREE' is a standard vector font with a drop shadow, lacking the jagged, hand-crafted charm of authentic 90s pixel type. expressiveness.suggestion: Abandon the 'window within a window' approach. The entire screen should be the game world. Replace the grey UI box with a semi-transparent, pixelated overlay or simply float the text directly over the snow. The 'START' button should be a diegetic pixel-art object—perhaps a wooden signpost or a stylized pixel button that looks like it belongs in the game's asset library, not a web browser.
